Senses.Explanation: Literally, a repeated, layered, or weighty barrier. The expression occurs 739 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Counts range from one to ten thousand barriers; one passes, breaks, opens, guards, or remains separated by them. The recurring warning says, ‘do not say no-mind is the Way; no-mind still leaves one further barrier.’ Speakers also ask who has passed it, request presentation of ‘the final barrier,’ and direct a questioner to ‘ask the gatekeeper.’ A late discourse gives its own named description of ‘passing through the further barrier’; this is preserved as that text’s account, not made universal. Zen bends the checkpoint image into a public measure, but the corpus names no fixed numbered stage shared by every use.
Senses.Note: Family check: “one further barrier” (一重關), “two barriers” (兩重關), “four barriers” (四重關), “a thousand and ten thousand barriers” (千重萬重), “the final formidable barrier” (末後重關), “the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ formidable barrier” (佛祖重關), and “pass through the formidable barrier” (透重關) vary scale or sequence, not referent. No split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫謂無心云是道，無心猶隔一重關。示眾，云：泥佛不度水，木佛不度火，金佛不度爐，真佛內裏坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 列祖提綱錄, Yuantong Daomin's hall-address sequence, identified by the self-reference 圓通. Yuantong is the exact speaker who warns not to call no-mind the Way because no-mind still lies beyond one heavy barrier.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：木馬衝開千騎路，鐵牛透過萬重關。木馬鐵牛，即今在甚麼處？良久曰：驚起暮天沙上雁，海門斜去兩三行
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷). Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), Shengshou Yongmin section. Shengshou Yongmin is the exact hall speaker who says that a wooden horse breaks open a road for a thousand riders and an iron ox passes through ten thousand layered barriers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「如何過得這重關？」師云：「問取把關吏。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 雪關禪師語錄, end-of-retreat public exchange. The exact headword-bearing speaker is an unnamed questioning monk: after Xueguan rejects his comparison of the retreats, the monk advances and asks how to pass this heavy barrier; Xueguan tells him to ask the barrier guard. The six-rung review found no personal name for this monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「大開爐煹，鋾鑄聖凡，末後重關，請師拈出。」師云：「但得雪消後，自然春到來。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 大休珠禪師語錄, opening-of-retreat public exchange. The exact headword-bearing speaker is an unnamed questioning monk: he asks Daxiu Zhu to bring out the final heavy barrier, and Daxiu answers that when the snow melts spring naturally arrives. The six-rung review found no personal name for this monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 境智融通，色空無礙，獲大自在，常住不動，是則名為透重關，名為大死大活者。透重關後，家舍即在途中，途中不離家舍
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 御選語錄, imperial general preface. The Yongzheng Emperor is the exact author: he defines penetrating the heavy barrier as the stage in which mountains, rivers, earth, and the elements are each themselves, and calls it great death and great life.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾中莫有透出重關者麼？出來與華藏相見。良久，云：無人知此意，令我憶南泉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 續古尊宿語要, Dun'an Zongyan section. Dun'an Zongyan is the exact Mid-Autumn hall speaker: after raising Hanshan's moon verse, he asks whether anyone can emerge through the heavy barrier and come meet Huazang, pauses, and remembers Nanquan.
